title: Understanding cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome (CKM): What the 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN guideline means for risk assessment, prevention, and integrated care
summary: In a Q&A with Medical Laboratory Observer, Dr. Leslie Saltzman, vice president of Consumer Health Solutions at Labcorp, discussed the Marker by Labcorp Genetic Health Panel and the role of hereditary genetic risk testing.
body_markdown:
## Key updates to the CKM care model


[Cardiovascular disease](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/cardiovascular/conditions/cardiovascular-disease) ,[chronic kidney disease](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/chronic-kidney-disease) , obesity, and type 2 diabetes are among the most prevalent and costly chronic conditions, negatively affecting health outcomes worldwide. Traditionally, these disorders have been managed as separate clinical entities. However, growing evidence demonstrates that they are closely interconnected and often develop through shared biological pathways. The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of CKM Syndrome introduces a new framework that recognizes these conditions as components of a single syndrome.1 The guideline emphasizes earlier identification of risk, coordinated management across specialties, and interventions that address multiple organ systems simultaneously.


Among the most significant updates are:


- Formal adoption of the CKM Syndrome staging framework
- Expanded use of the PREVENT risk equations
- Greater emphasis on obesity as an underlying driver of disease
- Integration of kidney, cardiovascular, metabolic, and liver health into routine risk assessment
- Increased use of cardioprotective and kidney-protective therapies in appropriate patients
- Recognition of interdisciplinary care as a key component of optimal outcomes


Together, these changes encourage a proactive, longitudinal approach to reducing cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic risk across the life course.


## Why the 2026 CKM guideline matters


Historically, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, and chronic kidney disease have been treated within separate clinical silos. Patients often move between primary care, cardiology, endocrinology, and nephrology, with each condition addressed independently.


The new guideline recognizes that these conditions are deeply interconnected and frequently progress together. Excess adiposity, insulin resistance, kidney dysfunction, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease form a continuum rather than isolated disorders. As a result, preventing progression at earlier stages may improve outcomes across multiple organ systems.


The committee writing the 2026 guideline describes the CKM care model as a shift toward more integrated, less siloed care for patients with interconnected cardiometabolic conditions.


## A new framework: CKM Syndrome


The defining feature of the guideline is the introduction of a unified CKM syndrome framework.


Rather than focusing on a single disease state, CKM Syndrome describes a continuum that spans[metabolic risk factors](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/cardiovascular/conditions/cardiometabolic-disease) , kidney disease, subclinical cardiovascular disease, and established cardiovascular disease. The framework is intended to support earlier intervention and more consistent risk assessment throughout a patient's lifetime.


## CKM Syndrome stages


**Stage** **Description**


0 No CKM risk factors present


1 Excess or dysfunctional adiposity and/or prediabetes


2 Metabolic risk factors, chronic kidney disease, or both


3 Subclinical cardiovascular disease or very high predicted cardiovascular risk


4 Clinical cardiovascular disease with CKM risk factors present


The guideline emphasizes that progression is not inevitable and intervention at earlier stages may prevent advancement to more serious disease.


## Modern risk assessment with PREVENT


Risk assessment is central to the CKM framework.


The guideline recommends the American Heart Association's PREVENT equations as the preferred tool for estimating cardiovascular risk. Unlike older models, PREVENT incorporates factors directly relevant to CKM Syndrome, including body mass index (BMI) and kidney function. Additional modules can incorporate[urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR)](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/140285/albumin-creatinine-ratio-random-urine) ,[hemoglobin A1c](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/001453/hemoglobin-hb-a1c) , and measures of social determinants of health.


Key advantages include:


- Assessment of both 10-year and 30-year risk
- Integration of cardiovascular and kidney risk factors
- Improved risk estimation across diverse patient populations
- Support for earlier intervention in younger adults with accumulating risk factors


The guideline encourages clinicians to move beyond single-disease assessment and evaluate risk across the entire CKM spectrum.


## Earlier detection across organ systems


A major theme throughout the guideline is identifying silent or early disease before clinical events occur.


The guideline highlights the importance of routinely assessing:


- Obesity and adiposity-related risk
- Prediabetes and diabetes
- Kidney function and albuminuria
- Cardiovascular risk factors
- Liver fibrosis risk in patients with metabolic disease


Of note, the guideline recommends periodic FIB-4 assessment in adults with diabetes or multiple cardiometabolic risk factors to evaluate risk for liver fibrosis associated with[metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/nash-mash) . This recommendation reinforces the growing recognition that liver health is an important component of overall cardiometabolic risk.


## Weight management as a foundation of CKM care


The guideline identifies[weight management](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/weight-loss-management) as a fundamental objective throughout the CKM continuum.


Lifestyle modification remains the foundation of care, including nutrition, physical activity, sleep health, and behavioral interventions. The document encourages clinicians to use a nonjudgmental, patient-centered approach when discussing weight and obesity.


Importantly, the guideline recognizes that obesity is not simply a risk factor for downstream disease. Instead, it is often a primary driver of CKM progression and should be addressed early to reduce future cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic complications.


## Kidney protection and cardiovascular prevention


The guideline places a strong emphasis on identifying chronic kidney disease earlier and treating albuminuria as an important marker of future risk.


uACR is highlighted as a critical tool for risk assessment and treatment decision-making. The guideline recommends ongoing monitoring of albuminuria and kidney function to assess residual risk and guide therapy.


More broadly, the document reinforces a growing body of evidence showing that interventions that protect kidney function often provide cardiovascular benefits as well, supporting a more integrated approach to patient management.


## The importance of coordinated care


Perhaps the most important practice-level message from the guideline is that CKM Syndrome cannot be managed effectively by a single specialty alone.


The writing committee formally recommends interdisciplinary care models involving primary care providers, cardiologists, nephrologists, endocrinologists, obesity specialists, pharmacists, dietitians, and other healthcare professionals as appropriate. Coordinated care and shared decision-making are viewed as critical components of improving long-term outcomes.


This recommendation reflects the reality that successful prevention often requires management of multiple interconnected conditions simultaneously rather than independently or sequentially.


## Practical implications for clinical practice


The 2026 CKM guideline encourages clinicians to:


**Think beyond individual diseases**


Evaluate cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic health together rather than separately.


**Assess risk earlier**


Identify obesity, prediabetes, albuminuria, and other risk factors before clinical disease develops.


**Use contemporary risk tools**


Incorporate PREVENT risk estimation and CKM staging into routine clinical assessment.


**Monitor multiple organ systems**


Consider cardiovascular, kidney, metabolic, and liver health as interconnected components of patient risk.


**Coordinate care**


Develop collaborative management strategies that address the full spectrum of CKM Syndrome.


## A new direction for chronic disease prevention


The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN Guideline for Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome represents a major evolution in chronic disease prevention and management. Rather than treating obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease as separate conditions, the guideline introduces a unified framework that recognizes their shared biology, cumulative impact on long-term health, and positive response to targeted interventions.


By emphasizing earlier detection, comprehensive risk assessment, coordinated multidisciplinary care, and lifelong prevention, the CKM framework provides clinicians with a practical approach to identifying at-risk individuals sooner and intervening before irreversible disease develops.


As implementation of the framework grows, the CKM model is expected to reshape how clinicians evaluate and manage cardiometabolic health across the continuum of care.
